verdict: OK to lend in Chakan auto OEM chain — pursue Tier-1/Tier-2 suppliers with EV-testing and export exposure, avoid single-OEM-dependent low-margin job-work units; structure tightly on receivables and commodity pass-through.
title: Chakan Cars & Commercial Vehicles (OEM): a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Chakan is an OEM-anchored cluster: a Skoda VW India car plant plus a ring of Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers feeding it. Capex is lumpy (presses, moulds, test rigs) and funded ahead of revenue, so the working-capital cycle — inventory plus receivable minus payable — is where the cash actually gets trapped. Collect the actual receivable days and inventory days from customer before you size any limit. ## What has changed now
**The local news is a capability upgrade, not a volume event.** Skoda VW India has signed an MoU with ARAI to transfer land next to its Chakan plant for an advanced crash-test facility covering both battery-electric and ICE vehicles, including Bharat NCAP and export tests [1][2][3]. That shortens EV development timelines and pulls testing demand into Chakan [1]. Read it as a signal that the OEM here is committing to EV and export programmes locally — good for suppliers who tool up for those programmes. It says nothing about order volumes; collect from customer. ## The numbers and the gap
**National output is running hot while credit is running hotter.** IIP for NIC 29 (motor vehicles) is +25.2% YoY and +19.2% Apr-to-date [D]. Bank credit to the sector is +27.0% YoY against that +19.2% output — a +7.8 pp gap [D]. Maharashtra GST is +8.6% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1% [D], so the local tax base is growing faster than the country. **That credit-output gap is the single most important thing on your desk: some of the borrowing is funding working capital for real volume, and some is funding inventory that isn't moving.** When a proposal lands, check whether the loan is against confirmed OEM purchase orders or against speculative build; if it's the latter, ask for the OEM schedule in writing. ## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers with a named EV or export programme at Chakan, and tooling/test-service vendors riding the ARAI facility.** Peer results support demand: M&M auto revenue +25% with EBIT margin at 9.5% [5], Tata Motors CV volumes +26% with price hikes flagged on commodity inflation [6], and export-focused OEMs expected to hold margins better [7]. Margins are the pressure point — Q4FY26 auto EBITDA growth ~21% but commodity risk flagged [4]. So structure limits against receivable, not against fixed assets; take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, monthly OEM payment advices, and a quarterly commodity pass-through confirmation. Avoid single-customer job-work units with no tooling ownership and no price-escalation clause. - **Inventory build without matching order book** — check monthly; if finished-goods days rise while dispatches fall, cut limit. - **Commodity cost not passed through** — check quarterly; if gross margin compresses two quarters running, reprice or exit.
